content.title: Domain, Range, and Graph Relationships of Inverse Functions
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the relationship between a function and its inverse. You will learn how to determine the domain and range of an inverse function by swapping the domain and range of the original function, and how to identify the graph of an inverse function using reflection across the line y = x.
learning_objectives: Identify the domain and range of a function f(x) by finding excluded values.
Determine the domain and range of the inverse function f⁻¹(x) by swapping the original domain and range.
Recognize the graphical relationship between a function and its inverse as a reflection across the line y = x.

sections.title: The Domain-Range Swap
sections.content:
The most fundamental rule of inverse functions is the swap: the domain of the original function f becomes the range of the inverse function f⁻¹, and the range of the original function f becomes the domain of the inverse function f⁻¹. If a value is excluded from the domain of f (for example, because it makes a denominator zero), that same value will be excluded from the range of f⁻¹.

![A flow chart showing the steps to find inverse domain and range: Find f domain, Find f range, Swap them for f-inverse.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/e1b794a0-678e-4560-a033-34f4d255d8bf-1786505935577-624.webp)

sections.title: Finding Excluded Values
sections.content: To find the domain of f, look for values that make the denominator zero or result in the square root of a negative number. To find the range of f, it is often helpful to solve the equation y = f(x) for x. The values that y cannot take in this new expression represent the excluded values of the range of f, which are the excluded values of the domain of f⁻¹.

sections.title: Graphical Reflections
sections.content: The graph of an inverse function f⁻¹ is a reflection of the graph of f across the identity line y = x. This means that if a point (a, b) exists on the graph of f, the point (b, a) must exist on the graph of f⁻¹.

worked_examples.question: Given f(x) = (2x + 3) / (x - 1), what is the domain of the inverse function f⁻¹(x)?
worked_examples.solution:
Step 1: Find the domain of f(x). The denominator x - 1 cannot be zero, so x ≠ 1. This means 1 is excluded from the domain of f (and thus excluded from the range of f⁻¹).
Step 2: Find the range of f(x) by solving y = (2x + 3) / (x - 1) for x.
Multiply both sides by (x - 1): y(x - 1) = 2x + 3
Distribute: xy - y = 2x + 3
Move x terms to one side: xy - 2x = y + 3
Factor out x: x(y - 2) = y + 3
Solve for x: x = (y + 3) / (y - 2).
Step 3: Identify excluded y-values. In the expression x = (y + 3) / (y - 2), the denominator cannot be zero, so y ≠ 2. This means 2 is excluded from the range of f.
Step 4: Swap. Since the range of f excludes 2, the domain of f⁻¹ excludes 2. Therefore, the domain of f⁻¹ is all real numbers except 2.

common_mistakes: Confusing the excluded domain value of f with the excluded domain value of f⁻¹. Remember: f's domain restriction affects f⁻¹'s range.
Thinking the inverse is a reflection across the x-axis or y-axis. It is always a reflection across the diagonal line y = x.
Forgetting to solve for x when the range of the original function is not immediately obvious.
exam_tips: If you are stuck, pick a point (a, b) that satisfies f(x) and check if (b, a) satisfies the options for f⁻¹.
For rational functions like f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d), the horizontal asymptote y = a/c is the value excluded from the range of f, and thus excluded from the domain of f⁻¹.
content.recap: To find the domain and range of an inverse, find the domain and range of the original function and swap them. Graphically, the inverse is always the reflection of the original function across the line y = x.

knowledge_claims.content: The domain of a function f is identical to the range of its inverse function f⁻¹.
The range of a function f is identical to the domain of its inverse function f⁻¹.
If a value k is excluded from the domain of f(x), then k is excluded from the range of f⁻¹(x).
If a value k is excluded from the range of f(x), then k is excluded from the domain of f⁻¹(x).
The graph of an inverse function f⁻¹ is the reflection of the graph of f across the line y = x.
To find the range of a function f(x) algebraically, solve the equation y = f(x) for x and identify values of y that make the resulting expression undefined.
If the point (a, b) lies on the graph of f, then the point (b, a) must lie on the graph of f⁻¹.
It is a mistake to assume the domain of f and the domain of f⁻¹ are the same; they are only the same if the domain and range of f are identical.
One can verify an inverse function's domain by checking the vertical asymptotes of the inverse function's equation.
For a rational function f(x) = (ax + b)/(cx + d), the value y = a/c is excluded from the range of f and therefore excluded from the domain of f⁻¹.
An excluded value in a domain is a value for which the function has no defined output, such as a value causing division by zero.
A reflection across the line y = x swaps the x and y coordinates of every point on the original graph.
